characters.name: Walk Clerk Eren
characters.role: Keeper of the Glass Walk notice

dialogue.speaker: voices-steward
dialogue.text: The glassmakers need the reopened path for their first delivery. The draft calls the public opening its first crossing. A carrier remembers taking the rail two days earlier. Bring me the signed entry and the carrier’s permission card before you change the heading.

dialogue.speaker: voices-steward
dialogue.text: The carrier dates the trial by the lamps coming on. The clerk dates public passage by the signature. Both can sit on the same board with their own headings.

options.text: Pin the two dated records under separate headings.
Leave the draft clipped up for now.
We left room on the Nexus date ribbon.
Where should we put the approved reading copy?

dialogue.speaker: voices-steward
dialogue.text: The patent peg had a day, and the museum sleeve covered years. They left the start of everyday use open. We can leave room on this board for when someone first crossed, too.

dialogue.speaker: voices-steward
dialogue.text: The trial goes on the Lantern 4 line with the carrier’s account. The public opening keeps the Lantern 6 date from the register. Leave a gap where a record of the first crossing would go.

dialogue.speaker: voices-steward
dialogue.text: Try both guide copies at the listening desk. The carrier’s local line starts at the quay, where people count lamps. The register tells us when the gates opened for public passage. Eren needs to know where the route line came from before it goes outside.

options.text: Leave the desk ready.
Where should we put the approved reading copy?

dialogue.speaker: voices-steward
dialogue.text: You have the dated lines and the plain directions. Clerk Eren can put the approved phrase next to the guide or keep it at this desk with the dates. The carrier gave us permission for that one phrase.

options.text: Leave the desk ready.
Where should we put the approved reading copy?

dialogue.speaker: voices-steward
dialogue.text: The excerpts and both guide copies stay here. The carrier’s permission card tells every clerk which phrase they may repeat. The empty line beside the two dates stays open for a record that could settle it.

options.text: Leave the desk ready.
Where should we put the approved reading copy?

dialogue.speaker: voices-clerk
dialogue.text: My stamp opened the path for public use. The crew could bring lamps along the rail before my desk opened. Take the signed Lantern 6 entry back to Wren.

dialogue.speaker: voices-clerk
dialogue.text: The quay crews ask for the words they use on the rail. New carriers ask for a short line they can read with both hands full. We have room for either notice. The archive can carry the dated records on both routes.

options.text: Keep the carrier’s wording beside a plain direction.
Put the short route guide on the walk.
Leave the board ready for now.

dialogue.speaker: voices-clerk
dialogue.text: Eren puts “Second lamp, then the rail” above the quay direction. The two dates have short source lines. A new carrier can match the words people call to each other on the quay and see who recalled the trial.

dialogue.speaker: voices-clerk
dialogue.text: Eren puts one direction on the board for someone carrying a crate. A small line sends curious readers to the dated records and the carrier’s approved words at Wren’s desk.

dialogue.speaker: voices-clerk
dialogue.text: There is a reply by the quay rail. A carrier came in from the stairs. Look at what stands in front of you from the stairs and the quay before you move the arrows.

dialogue.speaker: voices-clerk
dialogue.text: You saw lamps from the quay and the arch from the stairs. Both routes reach the same rail. We could give the two groups a marker they both see, or keep the quay line and give the stairs its own direction.

options.text: Use the arch and rail as shared markers.
Give each arrival point its own line.
Keep the notice ready.
A library reader asked us where they could reach a stop.

dialogue.speaker: voices-clerk
dialogue.text: Then you already know to start where the reader arrives. The library had a count without a reachable stop. We had a direction with one starting point. Put the markers where a person can use them.

options.text: Use the arch and rail as shared markers.
Give each arrival point its own line.
Keep the notice ready.

dialogue.speaker: voices-clerk
dialogue.text: Eren puts the arch and rail on the arrow above the two approaches. Someone coming in from either side can use those landmarks. The first notice stays on the public board and Wren keeps the dated records.

dialogue.speaker: voices-clerk
dialogue.text: Eren leaves the quay’s lamp line on the arrow from the water. A second arrow takes a reader from the stairs straight to the arch and rail. The first notice and both dated records stay available.

dialogue.speaker: voices-clerk
dialogue.text: A glassmaker stopped at the arch with a crate. They could see the arrow but had to lean over the rail to follow its small lines.

options.text: Put a larger card by the arch.
Leave the arrow where it is.

dialogue.speaker: voices-clerk
dialogue.text: Eren moves a broad copy onto the low rest at the arch. A carrier can set down a crate and follow the directions. Each date and source keeps a line of its own.

dialogue.speaker: voices-clerk
dialogue.text: The low card gives people room to look up and match a line to the path. The original excerpts are still at Wren’s desk.

dialogue.speaker: voices-steward
dialogue.text: A line forms at the desk when the boats come in. We can put the approved excerpt by the queue where someone can read while they wait. At the reading slot it can sit beside the record and permission. Which place should get the copy?

options.text: Give people in the queue an approved excerpt.
Keep the excerpt at the reading slot with its record.
Leave the copy with you for now.

dialogue.speaker: voices-steward
dialogue.text: Wren clips a short copy where the waiting line turns. It names the test walk and directs people to the record. A dock runner starts to read while the clerk helps someone else.

dialogue.speaker: voices-steward
dialogue.text: Wren clips the approved line to its date and permission at the reading slot. The first reader follows the clips to see what the carrier let the archive share. People behind them wait until the slot is free.

dialogue.speaker: voices-steward
dialogue.text: My father stayed by this lamp when I was late. I remember that his coat dripped for an hour. Tonight I can take one extra turn here. The small lamp has two brackets. Try the one by the rail and the one over the bench.

options.text: Hang the small lamp on the rail bracket.
Hang the same lamp above the waiting bench.
Tell Wren how you asked Ottilie about the Market shrine.
Tell Wren what you weighed beside the Market shrine.
Tell Wren what you kept in Sefa’s flood song.
Tell Wren what you found about the Nexus arch.
Leave the lamp here.

dialogue.speaker: voices-clerk
dialogue.text: From the waiting spot, that small lamp falls in line with the passage markers. The closed desk’s board is behind it. Someone on the quay could take the light as a sign that they can still check in.

options.text: Try the other bracket.
Step away from the brackets.

dialogue.speaker: voices-clerk
dialogue.text: From the same waiting spot, I can see the light on the seat. I can read “Check-in closed” at the rail past it. A person can reach the bench without going to the check-in desk.

options.text: Try the other bracket.
Step away from the brackets.

dialogue.speaker: voices-steward
dialogue.text: You asked Ottilie what her own promise meant. Ours gives the lamp a keeper and a place for a guest. You can still ask Eren what the desk’s board says.

options.text: Go back to the two brackets.

dialogue.speaker: voices-steward
dialogue.text: You put a town weight beside the stamped one. Here you can set the lamp beside the notice and see whether both can be read. The lamplighters can tell you what they want their light to say.

options.text: Go back to the two brackets.

dialogue.speaker: voices-steward
dialogue.text: You helped Sefa keep her grandmother’s verse and give the boats a verse as well. I thought of that when Eren hung the closing notice. Maybe two lines can do two jobs here too.

options.text: Go back to the two brackets.

dialogue.speaker: voices-steward
dialogue.text: You found the hope carved over the Nexus arch. My father used to joke that our lamp could do the waiting for him. Then he would take his wet coat and go sit right where you are standing.

options.text: Go back to the two brackets.

dialogue.speaker: voices-steward
dialogue.text: Stand at the reading-room threshold. The straight passage back to the quay is visible from here. The entrance has a seat and stays staffed through the reading turn, after Eren closes check-in. I can set the promise lamp here if the quay keeps a direction.

options.text: Pin a trial arrow and check that it points towards this door.
Leave the doorway as it is.

dialogue.speaker: voices-steward
dialogue.text: The trial arrow starts at the waiting bench and points to this door. Somebody who arrives tired still has the walk along the quay. The reading-room keeper has offered the seat and can be here during the ordinary reading turn.

dialogue.speaker: voices-clerk
dialogue.text: Put the folio on the treaty. The first window follows the land described in Article 1. The second picks out the parties named at the beginning and the marks at the end.

options.text: Slide from the land line to the parties and the fifth article.
Leave the treaty open.

dialogue.speaker: voices-clerk
dialogue.text: The transcript lists William Henry Harrison and names the marks under Delaware, Potawatomi, Miami and Eel River Miami headings. Those are the parties named here. Article 5 gives us a separate Wea agreement to look for. Turn to Tecumseh’s case for a recorded objection to the treaty.

dialogue.speaker: voices-steward
dialogue.text: The case has a public account from the Absentee Shawnee Tribe and a state marker from Indiana. The same name appears on both. Put the folio over each source line before moving its date.

options.text: Set the marker’s date apart from the dates of the meetings.
Leave the two sources beside each other.

dialogue.speaker: voices-steward
dialogue.text: The Absentee Shawnee Tribe describes how Tecumseh sought an alliance among Native nations. The 2011 state marker records his objections at Vincennes in 1810 and 1811. Give the account and marker their own sources. The wording of his speeches stays open in this display.

dialogue.speaker: voices-steward
dialogue.text: A visitor saw the territory line and told the next reader that everybody agreed to it. We can open the new copy at the article that sends people to a separate record. Or we can open it with the dates of Tecumseh’s challenge. Keep the other page easy to find.

options.text: Open at Article 5 and hinge the account beside it.
Open with the Vincennes meetings and keep the treaty facing them.
Leave the covers ready.

dialogue.speaker: voices-steward
dialogue.text: The first reader asks where the agreement named in Article 5 went. I pin a route note to Library Dispatch in the Civic Machine. Look for a second dated record there.

dialogue.speaker: voices-steward
dialogue.text: The first reader asks why Tecumseh challenged the treaty. I put the Absentee Shawnee account at the bench. The facing treaty page has a route note to the separately dated Civic copy.

missions.title: The Second Lamp
missions.knowledgeQuestion: How can a public sign carry a local account and help someone who arrives by another path?
missions.stake: If a remembered walk is filed as a record, the lantern opening is dated wrong for everyone after.

Read the permission card and register, then open both sources at the desk.

missions.title: The Edge of the Record
missions.knowledgeQuestion: Whose decision does a record show, and how can we tell whose it leaves open?

objectives.title: Fit the folio to both Voices records and find who each names.
Open the public pair at one source and leave the other in reach.
Take the folio to Civic Dispatch and check the second date and the constitutional title.
Post the source lines at Civic and see who uses them.

journal.text: The trial and the public opening have separate dates and sources. We kept the carrier’s approved words and used two approaches to check the direction. The date of the first crossing is still open.

journal.title: The edge of the record
journal.text: I kept Tecumseh’s challenge and the treaty’s listed parties on facing pages. At Civic I found the separate date for the Wea convention and kept a present-day constitution under the name its own government gives it. Each record had a different reach.

moments.did: You kept two dated records and used the carrier’s approved words.
moments.prompt: What did each person choose to put on the public board?

moments.did: You crossed to the other approach to check a reader’s reply.
moments.prompt: Which landmark can disappear when someone starts in another place?

moments.did: You put a copy near a place where a carrier can read it.
moments.prompt: What could someone see from the rest that they could miss at the rail?

chronicle.title: Two dates on the walk
chronicle.text: The carrier recalls a Lantern 4 trial. The public opening register starts on Lantern 6. Wren has kept the limits of both records visible.

chronicle.title: A route from both sides
chronicle.text: A reader arrived from the stairs. The walk now gives a direction from both approaches, with the first notice and the approved excerpts still available.

sources.title: Fort Wayne treaty, 7 Stat. 113
sources.locator: September 30, 1809. Preamble, Articles 1 and 5, and signature list.
sources.supports: The text names its parties and describes the land cessions it records. Article 5 calls for a separate Wea agreement for the first tract.

sources.title: Absentee Shawnee Tribe: public account of Tecumseh
sources.locator: Public introduction explaining the Tribe’s logo. Paragraph on Tecumseh.
sources.supports: The Tribe identifies Tecumseh as a Shawnee leader and describes his work to unite Native peoples who wanted to live under their own leaders and laws.

sources.title: Indiana Historical Bureau: Tecumseh and Harrison
sources.locator: 2011 state historical marker, sides 1 and 2, Vincennes, Indiana.
sources.supports: The marker places meetings in August 1810 and July 1811 and reports Tecumseh’s opposition to the 1809 Fort Wayne treaty.

sources.title: Eastern Shawnee Tribe of Oklahoma: History
sources.locator: Opening paragraph identifying the three federally recognized Shawnee governments.
sources.supports: The Tribe distinguishes its own government from the Absentee Shawnee Tribe and the Shawnee Tribe.

cards.title: Parties named at Fort Wayne
cards.text: The record of 30 September 1809 names the United States and representatives of the Delaware, Potawatomi, Miami and Eel River Miami as parties. Its fifth article requires a separate agreement with the Wea for the first tract.
cards.limits: The names identify who appears as a party in this document. The page gives only part of the history of the land, the negotiations and the different communities affected.

cards.title: Tecumseh and the contested agreement
cards.text: The Absentee Shawnee Tribe describes Tecumseh’s work to unite Native peoples under their own leaders and laws. The Indiana Historical Bureau records his visits to Vincennes in 1810 and 1811 and his objection to the Fort Wayne treaty.
cards.limits: The Tribe’s account gives its own public framing. The Indiana marker is a later state account. The two sources establish neither a verbatim speech nor a position for every Shawnee community.

exhibits.name: Fort Wayne treaty
exhibits.dateKind: Date of the written agreement at Fort Wayne. The publication and its proclamation have separate dates.
exhibits.summary: This catalogue view points to the parties at the top of the treaty and to Article 5. That article calls for a separate Wea agreement for the first tract.
exhibits.altText: Original illustration of a paper folio with two marked edges.

exhibits.name: Two published accounts of Tecumseh
exhibits.dateKind: The meeting dates belong to the events described by the state marker. The marker itself was installed in 2011. The public Absentee Shawnee account supplies a separate perspective.
exhibits.summary: The Absentee Shawnee Tribe describes Tecumseh as a Shawnee leader who worked to unite different Native peoples. The state marker describes his challenge to the Fort Wayne treaty at Vincennes.
exhibits.altText: Original illustration of a paper folio with two marked edges.

keepsakes.name: Record-Edge Folio
keepsakes.text: A transparent archive cover with separate windows for the date, the writer and the people a record names. The keepers made it for the public reading cases.
keepsakes.where: The Fort Wayne and Tecumseh cases in the Archive of Voices
keepsakes.use: Fit the folio over the dated record stands in Voices and Civic Library Dispatch.

equip.method: Compare who could speak for a decision
equip.hint: Use the riveted stands to keep a date with the record that gives it. Follow Article 5 to the Civic Library.
